_readme: Renso: this file (src/data/portfolio.json) is the one place to edit the facts on the site. It feeds the certificate cards, flip-card backs, certificate pop-up, education details, hero stats, internship snapshot, contact links and the printable resume. Any empty string or empty list renders NOTHING on the page, so only fill a slot with something true. resume.pdf = path of a 1-page PDF you add to the repo (for example assets/Casalme_Renso_Resume.pdf); while it is empty the hero button prints the built-in resume instead. ojt.hours = required OJT hours (e.g. '486 hours'); ojt.window = when you can start and end; ojt.setup = Onsite / Hybrid / Remote; ojt.commute = cities you can reach; ojt.moa = e.g. 'DLSL endorsement letter available'. certs[].verifyUrl = the Credly / NetAcad link that proves the certificate (the Cisco images show a Cert ID at the bottom); a 'Verify credential' button appears once it is set. about.story = one or two sentences in your own words about what pulled you into IT. education[].details = short bullet facts; elementary and secondary stay empty until you confirm them. projects[0] = the capstone case study (Projects section, skill evidence { project: 'capstone' }, printable resume, terminal `show vlan brief` / `cat capstone.md`); its vlans and rules come from the final paper (Tables 4, 12 and 13), so keep them matching the paper. mine[] is only what you did yourself; teamParts and results stay credited to the team. The hero '7 VLANs I Configured' stat is plain HTML in Hero.astro. analytics.goatcounter = your GoatCounter site code, if you decide to use it. Keep valid JSON: double quotes, no trailing commas.

about.story: My interest started in high school, when a CIT subject first introduced me to coding and the basics of information technology. I chose IT in college because it is in demand and because I genuinely wanted to learn it. Now in my fourth year, I want to keep growing in this field and gain real-world experience.

projects.title: Academic Wi-Fi Security System
projects.official: NIST Cybersecurity Framework Based Authentication, Network Segmentation, and Encrypted Session Monitoring System for the Academic Wi-Fi Network of Saint Joseph College of Rosario Batangas Inc.
projects.client: Saint Joseph College of Rosario Batangas Inc.
projects.team: Team of 4 · I built the system with one teammate
projects.problem: The school’s Wi-Fi was one flat network with voucher logins: no directory accounts, no separation between students, staff and servers, no intrusion detection and no live view of who was connected.
projects.solution: We replaced it with a segmented network. Users sign in through a captive portal with their Active Directory account, each one lands in the VLAN of their role, and a default-deny firewall decides what that VLAN can reach.

mine.text: Designed and configured the seven role-based VLANs on the 802.1Q managed switch and pfSense, with an IP addressing plan and a DHCP scope for each one.
Wrote the pfSense default-deny inter-VLAN rules, per-role bandwidth limits and DNS-based content filtering, with every blocked attempt logged.
Helped set up Active Directory on Windows Server 2022, which the portal uses through RADIUS over LDAPS to check passwords and assign the VLAN.

teamParts: NIST CSF 2.0 mapping and STRIDE threat register
Testing and documentation in Agile sprints
projects.resultsNote: Team results, from the test reports in the final paper. The security tests used Nmap, Wireshark and Windows network tools.
lessons: User acceptance testing had one participant per role (3 people), and the student representative rated the clarity of role-based access as Fair (3 of 5). The paper recommends a block page that says a site is restricted by policy, and a larger UAT during the pilot.
Every performance target was met at 100 concurrent users. In the extended load test, the 200- and 300-session steps fell below the 95% login-success target, so they are repeated in the pilot.
Still to verify on the school’s production network: WPA3-Enterprise and 802.11w on the access points, Snort throughput at 100 Mbps, and the remaining paths of the lateral-movement test matrix.
